title: DISCRETE MATH
body:
Discrete maths is the maths of things you can count: whole numbers, sets, arrangements,
graphs. No limits, no derivatives, nothing continuous. It matters for the degree because
every object a computer actually manipulates is discrete, and because this is where you
learn to **prove** a claim rather than test it on a few inputs.

The spine of the course is **[[Proof]]**. Everything else is material to practise on.
[[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]] is the course that cashes this in hardest: the
[[Pumping Lemma]] and the halting argument in [[Turing Machine]] are both
[[Proof By Contradiction]], and you cannot follow either without having done this first.

## Topics

### Proof technique

[[Proof]] · [[Direct Proof]] · [[Proof By Contradiction]] · [[Proof By Induction]] ·
[[Induction]]

Three techniques, chosen by the shape of the claim. [[Direct Proof]] walks from the
hypothesis to the conclusion. [[Proof By Contradiction]] assumes the opposite and breaks
something. [[Proof By Induction]] handles anything indexed by the naturals, which in
practice means anything recursive: [[Recursion]], [[Tree]], [[Merge Sort]]'s running time.
[[Induction]] is the shorter pointer note and names the *structural* variant that
[[Context-Free Grammars]] and [[Recursion]] lean on.

### Sets

[[Sets]]

Union, intersection, complement, subset, the empty set, and set-builder notation. This is
the vocabulary layer the rest of the degree assumes without re-teaching:
[[Languages]] in [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]] are *literally* sets of [[Strings]]
over an [[Alphabet]], and closure properties of [[Regular Expressions]] are set operations
in disguise.

### Counting

[[Permutation]] · [[Combination]]

Permutation counts arrangements (order matters), combination counts choices (order does
not). This is what turns "how bad is brute force" into a number: the reason a
[[Hamiltonian Cycle]] search is hopeless is that there are $n!$ orderings to try, and it
is the counting half of [[Asymptotic Analysis]] and [[Time Complexity]].

### Graphs

[[Graph]] · [[Vertices]] · [[Directed Graph]] · [[Weighted Graph]] ·
[[Adjacency Matrix]] · [[Adjacency List]] · [[Hamiltonian Cycle]]

A graph is a set of vertices plus a set of edges, so it is a set-theory object before it
is a data structure. The notes for all of this live in
[[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]], which owns the representation and the cost analysis; this
course owns the definitions and the proofs about them.

### Number theory

[[Division Algorithm]] · [[GCD and LCM]] · [[Prime Number]] · [[Integer]]

Written up in [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]] as C++ exercises, and formalised
here. The division algorithm is the statement that quotient and remainder exist and are
unique; Euclid's algorithm for the GCD is the standard first example of a proof by
induction that also happens to be code you can run.

Third rung: [[ABSTRACT ALGEBRA]] (MATH 2101) takes the same objects as **structure**.
[[Modular Arithmetic]] makes the congruence classes the objects, the gcd becomes a generator,
and primality becomes irreducibility.

### Boolean and representation

[[Boolean Representation]] · [[Base Conversion]] · [[Boolean Algebra]] ·
[[Binary Operations]]

The applied half, owned by [[COMPUTING MACHINERY]]. Binary is a positional number system,
and Boolean algebra is a two-element algebra with its own laws (De Morgan, distribution)
that get proved the same way anything else here does.

## Core Facts to Know

- A **proof** is an argument that a claim holds for *every* case, not a check of some cases.
- One counterexample disproves a universal claim; no number of examples proves one.
- [[Direct Proof]]: assume the hypothesis, derive the conclusion.
- [[Proof By Contradiction]]: assume the negation of the claim, derive something false.
- Contradiction is the technique of choice when the claim itself is a negative ("no such thing exists", "not regular", "irrational").
- [[Proof By Induction]] has two parts: the **base case** and the **inductive step**.
- The inductive step proves $P(k) \Rightarrow P(k+1)$; it does not prove $P(k+1)$ outright.
- Assuming $P(k)$ is the **inductive hypothesis**, and it is not circular reasoning.
- Skipping the base case makes the whole induction worthless.
- **Strong induction** assumes $P(1) \ldots P(k)$ rather than just $P(k)$.
- **Structural induction** is induction over how a recursive object is built, not over a number.
- A **set** is an unordered collection with no duplicates.
- $A \subseteq B$ means every element of $A$ is in $B$; $A = B$ means $A \subseteq B$ and $B \subseteq A$.
- Proving two sets equal by proving both inclusions is the standard set-equality proof.
- $|A \cup B| = |A| + |B| - |A \cap B|$, inclusion-exclusion for two sets.
- The empty set is a subset of every set.
- A set of $n$ elements has $2^n$ subsets, its power set.
- A [[Permutation]] counts arrangements: order matters.
- A [[Combination]] counts selections: order does not matter.
- $P(n, r) = \dfrac{n!}{(n-r)!}$
- $C(n, r) = \dfrac{n!}{r!\,(n-r)!}$
- $C(n, r) = \dfrac{P(n, r)}{r!}$: a combination is a permutation with the $r!$ orderings divided out.
- $C(n, r) = C(n, n-r)$: choosing what to take is the same as choosing what to leave.
- $0! = 1$.
- Permutations of $n$ distinct objects: $n!$.
- The [[Division Algorithm]]: for integers $a$ and $d > 0$ there are unique $q$ and $r$ with $a = qd + r$ and $0 \le r < d$.
- A [[Prime Number]] has exactly two divisors, 1 and itself; 1 is not prime.
- $\gcd(a, b) \times \operatorname{lcm}(a, b) = a \times b$.
- A [[Graph]] is a pair $(V, E)$: a set of vertices and a set of edges.
- The sum of all vertex degrees is twice the number of edges, so it is always even.

## Related courses

- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]], which is this course applied: [[Proof]] technique for
  every argument, [[Sets]] for [[Languages]], [[Proof By Contradiction]] for the
  [[Pumping Lemma]] and [[Undecidability]], [[Proof By Induction]] for
  [[Context-Free Grammars]] and [[Finite Automata]] constructions ([[DFA]], [[NFA]]).
- [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]]: [[Graph]], [[Tree]], [[Binary Search Tree]], and the
  counting behind [[Asymptotic Analysis]] and [[Time Complexity]].
- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]]: [[Division Algorithm]], [[GCD and LCM]],
  [[Prime Number]], [[Integer]], [[Recursion]]. The code half of the number theory here.
- [[COMPUTING MACHINERY]]: [[Base Conversion]], [[Boolean Representation]],
  [[Binary Operations]]. The applied half of the Boolean material.
- [[ALGORITHMS AND COMPLEXITY]]: [[NP-Complete]] and the counting arguments that say why a
  brute-force search space is the size it is.
- [[STATISTICS]] (MATH 2234): **this course supplies block 2 of that one whole.** Events are
  [[Sets]], the probability axioms are stated on sets, and [[Permutation]] and [[Combination]]
  are the numerator whenever outcomes are equally likely. [[Proof By Contradiction]] is also the
  skeleton of a [[Hypothesis Testing|significance test]]: assume $H_0$, derive something
  implausible, reject the assumption, with a probability attached instead of a certainty.
